next_steps: Share compatibility matrix CSV and raw bench results
Schedule pilot kickoff next Wed (internal alignment by Tue)
Provide cost estimate for 100k tokens/day hosted vs Dedicated
action_items: Jordan Patel - Produce shortlist of 5 model variants + quant profiles - Due: 2027-07-20
Alex Chen - Email SOC2 and Private deployment checklist - Due: 2027-07-16

summary: Redwood team demoed the model concordance matrix and a proposed benchmark sprint approach. Customer is evaluating open models for conversational summarization + retrieval augmentation. Main concerns: latency vs cost, VPC networking and KMS, and deterministic fallbacks. Team agreed to a short pilot and Redwood to share security docs and bench CSVs.
topics: Routing and fallback policies (hosted vs dedicated)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Jordan Patel, Renee Ortiz / Maya Singh, Liam O'Connor, Priya Rao
---
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, AE on the account, and with me is Jordan SE, and Renee from product.
[00:10] Maya Singh: hi thanks, excited. quick context: we're trying to pick an open model family for our conversational summarization flow — must run in low-latency, support long context and ideally be cheap enough to operate at scale.
[00:25] Jordan Patel: great, yeah so today's demo is focused on a "concordance matrix" — basically a way to map model capability, kernel/runtime compatibility, quantization friendliness, and bench signals into a single view. we'll show the console, the matrix filters, and then propose a benchmark sprint.
[00:40] Liam O'Connor: sounds good. we also need to understand private deployment constraints — VPC, customer-managed KMS, and whether the KV cache persists across restarts.
[00:52] Jordan Patel: noted. we'll address K M S / key mgmt and the cache behavior in the security slide and in the bench notes.
[01:08] Renee Ortiz: quick product note — in the console you can pin model variants to routes, and the concordance view is interactive so you can filter by latency SLOs, token cost, and hardware compatibility.
[01:25] Maya Singh: okay can you walk through a concrete example?
[01:30] Jordan Patel: yeah sure, opening the model catalog... so here we have models grouped by family, then columns for: per-token median latency (on T4/NVIDIA-like), quantization profile support (8-bit, 4-bit), kernel maturity (green/yellow/red), and bench score for summarization QA.
[01:52] [Jordan shares screen - minor audio lag]
[02:10] Jordan Patel: for example the 'FalconX-variant' here has good accuracy but red on kernel maturity for AMP kernels — which means might need custom kernel mapping for 4-bit quant. our runtime will automatically route to a compatible variant if a kernel isn't available, that's one of the fallback policies.
[02:35] Priya Rao: when you say route to compatible variant, is that transparent at the API level or do we need to change prompts/routes?
[02:42] Alex Chen: transparent — you can set policy to prefer low-latency variants and allow fallback to a higher-latency but cheaper model, or vice versa. it's a config per-route in the Console.
[02:55] Maya Singh: hmm latency numbers — are they measured at 1k token sequences or 128 tokens? our median payload is around 512 tokens.
[03:05] Jordan Patel: great question — the matrix includes both 128/512/2048 columns. the bench sprint we propose will focus on 512 median and a P95 tail at 1.5x to simulate spikes. we'll give you the raw CSV.
[03:25] Liam O'Connor: on accuracy, how do you compute the bench score — is it rouge, f1, or custom evals?
[03:30] Renee Ortiz: it's configurable. the catalog shows a composite score from reference evals we run plus optional customer-provided prompt sets. for your sprint we'd run your prompts through our eval harness and show regression alerts.
[03:45] Maya Singh: can you talk about cost modeling — we want to compare hosted token cost vs spinning Dedicated GPU fleet.
[03:51] Alex Chen: absolutely. in Optimize we show per-route unit economics: cost/token, estimated monthly spend at X qps, and suggestions like batching, cache TTL, and quant profiles to reach target cost. Dedicated has a commit model — we can simulate breakeven.
[04:10] Priya Rao: about batching — our real-time convo path can't batch more than 4 at once; does Redwood still give benefits?
[04:17] Jordan Patel: yes even small batching combined with prefix caching (we call it KV/prefix cache) reduces token compute for repeated context, especially in RAG flows. note the cache effectiveness column in the concordance matrix.
[04:35] [00:05 long silence then cross talk]
[04:42] Maya Singh: any gotchas with quantizing the models we shortlisted? we care about hallucination rate after 4-bit quant.
[04:50] Jordan Patel: you can see quant resilience scores; some models show minimal perf drop at 4-bit, others degrade. our bench sprint will include qualitative checks for hallucination with your prompts.
[05:05] Liam O'Connor: security — can you run Dedicated inside our VPC and have the control plane separated? also SSO and role-based access?
[05:15] Alex Chen: Dedicated and Private both support a customer-managed control plane. SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC is supported, and we have KMS integrations — we'll attach SOC2 docs and a network diagram after.
[05:30] Maya Singh: perfect. show us how you would narrow the catalog down to 3 candidates.
[05:35] Jordan Patel: step one: filter by kernel maturity (green/yellow), quant support at 4-bit/8-bit, and runtime latency under 250ms median at 512 tokens. step two: sort by bench summarization score and cost per token. step three: pick a risky variant as fallback for throughput.
[06:05] [Jordan clicks filters, list updates]
[06:21] Jordan Patel: now gaps: for models with yellow maturity we recommend a small kernel mapping effort during the sprint. our SEs can port the kernels; timeline 1-2 weeks for typical mapping.
[06:36] Priya Rao: that's fine. what's the sprint scope exactly? deliverables?
[06:40] Renee Ortiz: proposed 2-week sprint: week 1 — run ingestion of customer prompts, run accuracy+latency benches across 5 model variants (128/512/2048); week 2 — quant experiments, kernel mapping if needed, produce concordance matrix and recommendation plus cost simulation.
[06:58] Maya Singh: cost for the sprint?
[07:01] Alex Chen: we can run an initial lightweight sprint hosted for free as part of evaluation credits; if kernel work required we'll estimate hours for SE time.
[07:12] Liam O'Connor: about data retention during benching — do you persist customer prompts? are they purged?
[07:18] Jordan Patel: logs are ephemeral for hosted evals; for Dedicated/Private you can run the bench in your VPC. we'll include a bench runner that can be executed in your environment to avoid data transfer.
[07:33] Priya Rao: okay nice. any mention of regen when fallback triggers — how transparent is the client to that?
[07:38] Alex Chen: the trace includes model variant and kernel metadata; and the Console shows route-level fallback incidents. we can also bubble alerts to Slack.
[07:48] [08:00] Jordan Patel: now demoing the bench CSV — here are columns: model, variant, seq_len, median_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, tokens_per_cost_unit, summarization_f1, rougeL, hallucination_flag_rate.
[08:14] Maya Singh: can I get that CSV after the call?
[08:17] Alex Chen: yes we'll send it.
[08:20] [08:30] Maya Singh: small observation — some of your labels for kernel maturity show cryptic terms, like 'SM-K' — what does that mean?
[08:35] Jordan Patel: sorry, shorthand — SM-K is our internal kernel compatibility class. we'll include the glossary in the sheet.
[08:42] Liam O'Connor: do you have customers using this for RAG in production? any case study?
[08:47] Renee Ortiz: we have a couple — one in finance with strict latency SLOs using Dedicated and a fallback routing policy. we'll share an anonymized case study.
[09:00] Maya Singh: switching to API ergonomics — our devs prefer simple REST with SDKs for Node/Python. can you show snippets?
[09:08] Alex Chen: sure, Console -> API keys -> route config. snippet: fetch('/v1/generate', { model: 'xxx', prompt,...}) — also SDKs handle streaming and tool calls.
[09:20] Priya Rao: about streaming — our UI needs partial tokens as they arrive, any issue with batching?
[09:26] Jordan Patel: we support partial streaming even with batching by interleaving the batch responses, latency SLOs are preserved using eager streaming mode.
[09:35] Maya Singh: good. on observability, we need trace-level cost per token by user and per-route P95.
[09:43] Renee Ortiz: Console has token-level cost breakdown, per-route dashboards, and we can export traces to your datadog.
[09:52] Liam O'Connor: what about audit logs and retention windows for compliance?
[09:56] Alex Chen: configurable retention; enterprise tier supports 7 years, default shorter retention. we'll include retention options in the appendix.
[10:12] [10:20] Maya Singh: two tough questions — 1) if we move to Dedicated and then switch models frequently, do we need to reprovision GPUs often? 2) what's the model rollover story?
[10:32] Jordan Patel: good ones. 1) Dedicated supports pinned pools and dynamic variant routing; you don't reprovision for a model that fits the same hardware profile. 2) rollouts are versioned, canary deployed, and we have automatic fallback to previous model if regression is detected.
[10:50] Priya Rao: regression detection — is that automatic with our evals?
[10:54] Renee Ortiz: yes, you can upload a golden set and define thresholds that trigger rollback or alerts.
[11:05] [11:20] Maya Singh: okay, show me an example concordance matrix exported for a shortlist.
[11:27] Jordan Patel: exporting now... CSV preview: rows with model names obfuscated — columns for confidence intervals for latency, quant stability, bench score.
[11:40] Maya Singh: I see a model with great bench score but red on quant stability — what's your recommendation?
[11:44] Jordan Patel: either keep it as low-latency hosted route (no quant), or pick a slightly lower-accuracy variant that's quant-friendly. tradeoff depends on your error tolerance.
[11:58] Liam O'Connor: what about multi-region fallbacks? if a region is full, do you route to another region with slightly higher latency or to a cheaper model?
[12:08] Alex Chen: routing policy is composable — you can prefer same-region low-latency, then fall back to cross-region equivalent, then to cheaper variant. Priorities and SLAs drive policy.
[12:25] Maya Singh: ok we're mostly convinced. what's the pricing delta if we choose a quantized 4-bit variant hosted vs Dedicated with A100s for our 100k tokens/day estimate?
[12:36] Alex Chen: we'll produce an apples-to-apples comparison in the cost sheet. rough ballpark: hosted quantized could be ~30-40% cheaper per token for this workload but Dedicated can beat hosted at steady high throughput depending on commit level.
[12:55] Priya Rao: do you support HSM-based key stores for KMS?
[12:59] Jordan Patel: yes HSM via partner KMS is supported for Private deployments, for Hosted we integrate with major cloud KMS providers.
[13:10] [13:20] Maya Singh: any red flags for us specifically?
[13:24] Alex Chen: only one: a few shortlisted models need kernel mapping for 4-bit; that is fixable but adds SE time. Otherwise the architecture fits.
[13:35] Liam O'Connor: timeline if we start pilot next week?
[13:38] Renee Ortiz: pilot kickoff + discovery day in week 1, bench run week 2, recommendation at end of week 2. so ~2 weeks end-to-end for the sprint.
[13:50] Maya Singh: that works.
[13:52] Alex Chen: recap of next steps: we'll send CSV + glossary + SOC2 pack and draft sprint plan. Jordan will put together shortlist and quant profiles.
[14:05] Maya Singh: perfect. thanks everyone.
[14:10] [closing chatter and goodbyes]
---
